sentences.text: The only known fossil of Tendaguripterus is a single dentary, or lower jaw, found in the Tendaguru Formation in southeastern Tanzania. This specimen, catalogued as MB.R.1290, serves as the holotype and is the sole basis for the species description. It is a tooth-bearing mandible that preserves parts of the skull and lower jaw.

The preserved dentary is short, robust, and tall, containing four tooth sockets and two incomplete teeth. The fragment measures 25.9 cm in length and reaches a depth of 9.9 cm at its deepest point near the back.

The lower jaw becomes over 1.5 times deeper at the back than at the front, creating an extremely deep shape. Unlike other dsungaripteroids, the teeth of Tendaguripterus project backward rather than upward or forward. The teeth in the posterior section of the fossil fragment point significantly backward.

Based on comparisons with Germanodactylus, the wingspan of Tendaguripterus is estimated to be about 1 meter wide. In 1999, Unwin and Heinrich estimated the complete skull length at 20 cm and the wingspan at 1 meter.

German fossil collectors discovered the specimen between 1910 and 1912 at Site Jg during an expedition to the Tendaguru Formation. Fossil material of Tendaguripterus was collected during German expeditions between 1909 and 1913 and identified by Hans Reck in 1931.

Paleontologists David Unwin and Wolf-Dieter Heinrich formally described the fossil as a new genus and species in 1999. The genus Tendaguripterus was named in 1999 by David Unwin and Wolf-Dieter Heinrich.
The species was named Tendaguripterus recki in honor of the German geologist Hans Reck. The type species of the genus is Tendaguripterus recki.

Researchers have proposed that Tendaguripterus was a durophage that fed on hard-shelled invertebrates like bivalves. Researchers suggest Tendaguripterus likely ate bivalves and other hard-shelled invertebrates.
The genus name combines "Tendaguru", the location of discovery, and the Greek word for wing. The genus authority for Tendaguripterus is Unwin & Heinrich, 1999.

In 2007, Alexander Kellner and colleagues argued that the resemblance between Tendaguripterus and other dsungaripteroids was superficial. Kellner and colleagues noted that Tendaguripterus lacks definitive traits of Dsungaripteroidea and cannot be confirmed as a pterodactyloid. Kellner and colleagues established the new family Tendaguripteridae to contain Tendaguripterus exclusively. In 2007, Alexander Kellner argued that Tendaguripterus's resemblance to Germanodactylus and Dsungaripterus was superficial and that it might not belong to Pterodactyloidea but rather be a more basal pterosaur. Based on Kellner's analysis, Tendaguripterus is placed in the undefined clade Tendaguripteridae, of which it is the only known member.
Tendaguripterus lived during the Late Kimmeridgian to Early Tithonian stages of the Late Jurassic period (152.21 to 149.2 million years ago).
Tendaguripterus fossils come from the Late Jurassic Tendaguru Formation in southeastern Tanzania, specifically from the late Kimmeridgian age within the Middle Saurian Member of the formation.

Tendaguripterus lived alongside dinosaurs such as Giraffatitan and Kentrosaurus, as well as other pterosaurs like Rhamphorhynchus and Pterodactylus. The ecosystem where Tendaguripterus lived included shallow marine lagoons, tidal flats, and vegetated inland areas.
It remains unclear whether Tendaguripterus belongs to Dsungaripteroidea or another group, as it has not been included in recent phylogenetic analyses.
